text: Probing Phosphorus Solubility and its Effect on Critical
Temperature (TC) in the Helical Superconducting Magnet
RbEuFe4As4-xPx
Mohammad Usman,1,2 Xiuquan Zhou,1 Christos D. Malliakas,2 Ulrich Welp,1 Wai-Kwong
Kwok,1 Duck Young Chung,1 and Mercouri G. Kanatzidis*,1,2
1Materials Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, Illinois 60439, United
States
2Department of Chemistry, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208, United States
*Corresponding Author: Mercouri G. Kanatzidis (E-mail: m-kanatzidis@northwestern.edu)
Abstract: RbEuFe4As4 exhibits a rare combination of high-temperature superconductivity and
non-collinear magnetism, originating from the FeAs and Eu layers, respectively. In order to fine-
tune its superconducting and magnetic properties, we studied P-doped RbEuFe4As4-xPx. To
determine the value of x for which RbEuFe4As4-xPx exists, members of the series have been
synthesized in the form of relatively large-sized single crystals by high-temperature flux growth
technique using RbAs flux as well polycrystalline powder by direct combination reactions between
RbFe2As2 and EuFe2As2-xPx. The flux crystal growth reactions indicate that RbEuFe4As4-xPx forms
with the values of x ≤ 0.12 which is corroborated by Rietveld refinement analysis on the products
obtained from direct combination reactions. The solubility limit exists primarily due to the
preferential site As(2) occupation by P in the RbEuFe4As4 crystal structure. As x increases in
RbEuFe4As4-xPx, magnetization measurements reveal that the superconducting critical transition
temperature (Tc) decreases while the magnetic ordering temperature (TN) remains almost
unchanged in comparison to undoped RbEuFe4As4.
Introduction
The discovery of layered, Eu-containing compounds of composition AEuFe4As4 (A = Rb,
Cs) (1144 compounds, for short) has introduced new members to the family of materials that
display superconductivity coexisting with three-dimensional long-range local moment magnetic
order. [1–6] Eu2+ ions carry a large, spin-only moment of 7 µB and enter a long-range ordered state
at TN = 15 K. The moments have an easy-plane anisotropy and order ferromagnetically within one
Eu-plane and exhibit a helical stacking with a period of four c-axis lattice constant along the c-
axis. [7,8] The superconducting transition occurs at Tc ~ 36.5 – 37.0 K. [2–4,9] Next to EuFe2As2
derived materials [10] and the family of (Li1-xMx)OH-intercalated FeSe (M = Fe, Mn, Co; Tc = 43
K) [11,12], RbEuFe4As4 has the highest Tc of any magnetic superconductor. The Eu-Fe-based
1144 superconductors are unique because they simultaneously display two mutually antagonistic
physical orders, high magnetic ordering and superconductivity, implying sizable magnetic
exchange interactions in the presence of strong superconducting pairing. Furthermore, the helical
magnetic structure may induce topological states and Majorana zero-modes on the c-surfaces of
AEuFe4As4 [13] the realization of which depends on the interplay of the magnetic exchange energy
and the superconducting gap. Previous work on Eu-1144 [14,15] has shown that the application of
hydrostatic pressure induces a decrease of Tc and an increase of TC such that they become
approximately equal near 7 GPa, thereby opening a way to tune the magnetic and superconducting
energy scales. Alternatively, work on inducing superconductivity by iso-valent P substitution in
EuFe2(As1-xPx)2 (Eu-122) compounds revealed that the primary effect of P substitution is the
generation of chemical pressure. [10] A highly stoichiometric form of RbEuFe4As4 is intrinsically
doped with approximately 1/4 hole per Fe, which is in line with the optimal substitution levels
observed in the 122 compounds. It is expected that introducing relatively low levels of P-doping
in RbEuFe4As4-xPx will result in a decrease in Tc and an increase in TN, which could create
conditions conducive to the emergence of topological states and other exotic situations where the
two orders occur at the same temperature, leading to fascinating phenomena.
Herein, we present a detailed investigation of the system of RbEuFe4As4-xPx using direct
combination reactions and flux synthesis methods. We found a relatively low solubility limit of x
~ 0.12 beyond which the 1144 structure does not crystallize. This is in sharp contrast to the
complete solubility of phosphorus in EuFe2As2, giving access to the full series EuFe2As2-xPx. X-
ray diffraction reveals that this limit arises due to the asymmetric surrounding of the Fe2As2 layers
such that the As(1) site faces the (smaller) Eu2+ ions whereas As(2) faces the larger Rb+ ions in the
RbEuFe4As4 crystal structure. The solubility is limited by the preferential incorporation of the
smaller (than As) P-ion on the As(2) site. At higher values of x, other phases, such as EuFe2As2
and Fe2As1-xPx appear. Magnetization measurements reveal that with increasing x-values, Tc
decreases from 36.8 K for undoped RbEuFe4As4 to 35.2(1) K in RbEuFe4As3.88(3)P0.12(3) while TN
is essentially unchanged at 14.5(2) K.
Experimental Section
Methods and Materials
Rubidium metal sealed under argon (99%, Johnson Matthey), europium chunks (99.9%,
Alfa Aesar), iron powder (99.998% Alfa Aesar), red phosphorus powder (99%, Beantown
Chemical), and arsenic powder (99.9999% Alfa Aesar) were used for the synthesis of all starting
materials. All reactions were carried out in alumina crucibles placed in evacuated fused silica tubes
sealed under a vacuum below 10-3 mbar and employed binaries and ternaries instead of using pure
elements for the ease of handling and safety purposes. Synthetic operations were carried out under
an argon atmosphere in an M-Braun glovebox with O2 and H2O concentrations at <0.1 ppm.
Caution! The syntheses of RbAs and RbP are nontrivial and extreme caution must be taken during
their loading, synthesis, handling, and disposal. Pnicogens and alkali metals (K and Rb) may react
spontaneously even in the glovebox during loading.
Direct Combination Reactions
RbAs was synthesized by directly combining Rb and As, on an approximately 10 g scale.
The mixture loaded in an alumina crucible and sealed in a fused silica ampoule was heated at a
rate of 8 °C/h to 200 °C, held there for 24-36 h, after which the furnace was turned off. RbP was
synthesized similarly, albeit using a slower heating rate of 3-5 °C/h. Upon reaction completion,
the ampoule was carefully opened in the glovebox and black granular powder was collected as
product which was homogenized thoroughly before use.
EuAs1-xPx and Fe2As1-xPx binaries were prepared by heating a stoichiometric mixture of
the elements in a fused silica ampoule at 800 °C for 24 h. RbFe2As2 was synthesized by directly
combining RbAs and Fe2As in an alumina crucible sealed in a Nb tube under argon atmosphere by
arc welding. The Nb tube was finally placed in a large, fused silica ampoule (18 mm OD and 16
mm ID). The pictorial description of this assembly is reported elsewhere. [4]The mixture in the
tube was heated to 800 °C in 24 h and held there for 48 h, followed by shutting the furnace off.
Similarly, RbFe2P2 was synthesized by heating a mixture of RbP and Fe2P in a similar tube
assembly but using a lower dwelling temperature 600 °C.
EuFe2As2-xPx ternaries were synthesized by loading a stoichiometric mixture of small Eu
pieces and Fe, As and red P powders in a fused silica ampoule, which was flame-sealed under
vacuum and heated to 900 °C in 12 h, and held there for 24 h, followed by shutting off the furnace.
The product was homogenized and reannealed two more times for each composition.
Crystal Growth
RbEuFe4As3.91(3)P0.09(3) and RbEuFe4As3.88(4)P0.12(4) were crystallized out of a RbAs flux by
layering a homogenized mixture of RbFe2As2 (0.15 g), EuFe2As1.75P0.25 (0.174 g), RbFe2As2 (0.15
g), and of EuFe2As1.5P0.5 (0.174 g) under RbAs (1.50 g) in an alumina crucible which was later
sealed in a Nb tube under an argon atmosphere. The Nb tube was sealed in an evacuated fused-
silica ampoule (18 mm OD, 16 mm ID). The reaction mixture was heated to 920 °C in 20 h, soaked
for 12–24 h, slowly cooled to 500 °C at a rate of 2 °C/h at which point the furnace was shut off.
Crystals measuring approximately 0.05 mm in size (Figure 1) were harvested for both
compositions. RbEuFe4As4-xPx crystals can also be synthesized using P-doped EuAs and Fe2As
binaries, but this approach, so far, has not proven successful in offering good control over
circumventing the formation of RbFe2As2 that typically forms as a parasitic phase in 1144
reactions. [4] After completion of the reaction, the remaining RbAs flux in the final product was
washed off using a 70/30 water/methanol mixture in a fume hood under N2 gas flow. It is important
that the reaction is worked-up under N2 flow as the product might contain pyrophoric residues.
Single Crystal X-ray Diffraction
Intensity data of plate-like black single crystals were collected at 100 K. Suitable single
crystals were mounted on a glass fiber with paratone oil on a Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy
diffractometer equipped with a micro-focus sealed X-ray tube PhotonJet (Mo) X-ray source and a
Hybrid Pixel Array Detector (HyPix) detector. The temperature of the crystal was controlled with
an Oxford Cryosystems low-temperature device. Data reduction was performed with the
CrysAlisPro software using an empirical absorption correction. The structure was solved with the
ShelXS structure solution program using the direct methods solution method and by using Olex2
as the graphical interface. [16] The model was refined with ShelXL [17] using least squares
minimization. Crystallographic refinement data and the atomic coordinates for
RbEuFe4As3.91(3)P0.09(3) and RbEuFe4As3.88(4)P0.12(4) are listed in Tables 1 and 2, respectively.
Scanning Electron Microscopy and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy
Surface imaging and the elemental analysis of RbEuFe4As4-xPx crystals were performed
using a Hitachi S-4700-II scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an energy-
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector. The samples were mounted on an aluminum sample
stub coated with carbon tape. The acceleration voltage and beam current used for the
measurements were 20 keV and 10 μA, respectively. EDS analyses, shown in Figures S1,
performed on multiple crystals gave the average compositions, Rb0.99Eu0.76Fe4As4.15P0.02 and
Rb0.91Eu0.82Fe4As4.24P0.08 for RbEuFe4As3.91(3)P0.09(3) (nominal composition: RbEuFe4As3.75P0.25)
and RbEuFe4As3.88(4)P0.12(4) (nominal composition: RbEuFe4As3.5P0.5), respectively. As shown in
Figure 1, the morphology of RbEuFe4As4-xPx crystals is nearly rectangular consistent with
RbEuFe4As4.
Powder X-ray Diffraction
Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) was used to assess phase purity using a Rigaku Miniflex
diffractometer with a Ni-filtered Cu Kα source (15 mA and 40 kV). Continuous scanning and
spinning were utilized with a step size of 0.02°. Finely ground powders were dispersed on a flat
sample holder to check for phase identification. Phase fraction and reaction completeness were
verified with synchrotron X-ray diffraction at 11-BM (λ = 0.4137 Å, 30 keV) at the Advanced
Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratory. Phase fractions for all samples were obtained by
analyzing the powder data with the General Structure Analysis System II package. [18]
RbEuFe4As4-xPx powders were sieved and loaded into Kapton capillaries sealed with clay at both
ends. For lattice constant determinations, powder diffraction data were analyzed using Rietveld
refinement and sequential refinements in Jana2006. [19] The data are shown in Figure 2.
Magnetization Measurements
The magnetic and superconducting transition temperatures of polycrystalline samples with
various P-substitution levels are deduced from measurements of the temperature dependence of
their magnetization. The magnetic measurements were performed in a MPMS3 SQUID
magnetometer manufactured by Quantum Design Inc. after cooling the sample in zero-field to 2
K, applying a field of 100 Oe, and recording the magnetic moment while the samples were warmed
up to 50 K. For these measurements, the powder samples were sealed in a non-magnetic plastic
capsule. The capsule is supported in a straw which, in turn, is mounted to the SQUID sample
holder. Through a repeated purge cycle at room temperature, air is removed from the powder
sample through a small opening in the lid of the capsule.
Results and Discussion
Direct Combination Reactions for RbEuFe4As4-xPx
All reactions presented vide infra were carried out in Nb tubes arc-welded under an argon
atmosphere and sealed in a fused silica tube. We began by carrying out a series of direct
combination reactions for x = 1, 2, 3, 4 in RbEuFe4As4-xPx. Table S1 summarizes the reagents used
for these reactions. The starting materials for each reaction were homogenized in an agate mortar
and pestle and heated to 850 °C in 12 h, dwelled for 84 h followed by shutting the furnace off. For
each reaction, black polycrystalline powder was obtained as a product which was homogenized
and reannealed at 850 °C for 48 h. Post completion, the resulting product for each reaction was
analyzed using PXRD and the diffraction patterns are shown in Figure 3 (top) revealing no
evidence for the formation of the desired RbEuFe4As4-xPx phase. However, these diffraction
patterns largely match the calculated pattern for EuFe2P2. We anticipate these products to be the
“disordered” or solid solution phases in the form of (Rb/Eu)2Fe4(As/P)4. Although these reactions
did not afford the desired P-doped 1144 phase, they indicated a potential limit, x<1, to the
phosphorus solubility in RbEuFe4As4-xPx. To further investigate the validity of this hypothesis, a
new series of direct combination reactions targeting smaller x-values in RbEuFe4As4-xPx (0<x≤1),
listed in Table S2, was carried out using reaction conditions as described above. The masses of the
reactants and products were recorded to ensure no significant material loss occurred during the
annealing process. Figure 3 (bottom) shows the PXRD patterns for the as-synthesized
RbEuFe4As4-xPx (0<x≤1) nominal compositions. All reactions, with the exception to that
nominated for RbEuFe4As3P, afforded the desired 1144 product as the major phase with small
amounts of EuFe2As2 forming as a side product. These findings indicated that the nominal P limit
in RbEuFe4As4-xPx might be close to x ≈ 0.75. In order to determine the actual phosphorus content
in the nominal compositions, RbEuFe4As3.75P0.25, RbEuFe4As3.5P0.5 and RbEuFe4As3.25P0.75,
Rietveld refinement analysis was performed on each of the three samples and the data are provided
in Table 3. With this information in hand, described in detail below, the next step was the synthesis
of high-quality single crystals for physical property measurements and accurate structural analysis.
Crystal Growth of RbEuFe4As3.91(3)P0.09(3) and RbEuFe4As3.88(4)P0.12(4)
RbAs has been shown to be an effective flux to crystallize complex alkali metal-containing
pnictides, especially arsenides, [4,20] due to its high reactivity and relatively low melting point of
575 °C. [21]The extreme reactivity of RbAs with quartz necessitates its use in an alumina crucible
sealed in Nb or other metal tubes. RbAs reacts with Nb to produce NbAs and to prevent this the
alumina container containing the starting materials, including RbAs must be plugged to prevent
RbAs from escaping the reaction mixture at elevated temperatures. The starting materials and
conditions for all flux crystal growth reactions are provided in Table S3. It is interesting to note
that for pure RbEuFe4As4 crystal growth, binary precursors, EuAs and Fe2As, afforded larger
crystals in higher yields compared to using the ternary precursor EuFe2As2 in RbAs flux. This may
be attributed to the higher solubility of the binary reagents in RbAs relative to EuFe2As2. However,
in contrast to these observations, for P-doped RbEuFe4As4, P-doped binaries, EuAs1-xPx and
Fe2As1-xPx, have so far, failed to consistently afford the desired RbEuFe4As4-xPx phase. In this case,
combining the P-doped ternary, EuFe2As2-xPx, with RbFe2As2 proved to be a more conducive
approach to growing RbEuFe4As4-xPx single crystals, although they are less than 0.1 mm in size as
shown in Figure 1. Future experiments aim to optimize the reaction conditions for growing larger
RbEuFe4As4-xPx single crystals to realize their advanced physical property measurements. Because
of the lower solubility of ternary starting precursors in molten RbAs as compared to binaries, the
mass of RbAs flux was increased to 22-fold to crystallize RbEuFe4As4-xPx, in contrast to pure
RbEuFe4As4, which can typically be crystallized out of a 8-15-fold excess of RbAs.
Crystal Structure of RbEuFe4As4-xPx and Phosphorus Solubility Limit
The 1144 compounds evolve from the 122 structure-types by introducing alternating
hetero-cationic layers. In other words, the 1144 phase is an accurate representation of ordered
stacking as opposed to disordered substitution. The main crystallographic difference between the
122 and the 1144 families is the lack of the n-glide plane across the Fe-layer in 1144 compounds,
and this causes the reduction of their symmetry from I4/mmm in 122 phases to P4/mmm. The
reduction of symmetry that is caused by the ordered stacking of two 122 phases to form a single
heterolayered 1144 phase may prove important in establishing the topological properties of the
material and the possible realization of Majorana zero modes. [13] [22–24]
In general, the formation of any ordered AEuFe4As4 (A = Rb, Cs) phase requires an ab
plane lattice match between AFe2As2 and EuFe2As2, as well as a large ionic difference between
A+ and Eu2+ ions. [25] RbEuFe4As4 can be described as an intergrowth structure of RbFe2As2 and
EuFe2As2 such that the Eu atoms end up forming a primitive tetragonal lattice running parallel to
the c-axis instead of being body-centered as in EuFe2As2 or EuFe2P2. Figure 4 illustrates the
crystals structure of RbEuFe4As4-xPx which is isostructural to RbEuFe4As4 with its unit cell
consisting of stacked Fe(As/P)4 layers sandwiched by layers of Eu2+ and Rb+ cations that alternate
along the c-axis. As shown in the figure, the Eu2+ and Rb+ cations in RbEuFe4As4-xPx are
coordinated to eight As(1) and As(2) atoms, respectively. The most crucial observation made in
this work is the preferential occupation of the As(2) site by P when doping RbEuFe4As4 with P
using direct combination reactions and/or flux crystal growth methods. As(2) sites form the layers
that sandwich the Eu2+ ions while Rb+ ions are intercalated between As(1) layers. A physically
plausible explanation for such preferential site occupation can be attributed to the size difference
between the ionic radii for Eu2+ and Rb+ cations. Eu2+ and Rb+ ions featuring 8-fold coordination
have ionic radii of 1.25 Å and 1.61 Å, respectively. [26] The smaller size of the Eu2+ ions between
the As(2) layers permits the substitution of the As(2) sites with P. Rb+ due to its relatively larger
ionic radius, allowing for the virtually negligible occupation of the As(1) layers by P. Several
crystals of composition RbEuFe4As3.91(3)P0.09(3)

One key structural parameter contributing to the high Tc of iron arsenide-based
superconductors is the high symmetry of tetrahedral FeAs4 units in the iron arsenide layers. [27]

high regularity. In contrast, the As–Fe–As bond angles in RbEuFe4As4-xPx are slightly different.

Superconducting Properties
Figure 5 shows the dc magnetic susceptibility data for polycrystalline RbEuFe4As4-xPx and
single crystal RbEuFe4As4-xPx. Pure RbEuFe4As4 exhibits a steep superconducting transition with
an onset temperature Tc = 36.8 K. Similarly, very sharp superconducting diamagnetic signals can
be seen in the figure with onset temperatures of 35.5 K, 35.08 K and 34.38 K for the nominal
compositions RbEuFe4As3.75P0.25, RbEuFe4As3.5P0.5 and RbEuFe4As3.25P0.75, respectively, and
35.2(1) K for single crystal RbEuFe4As4-xPx (xcalc = 0.09(3) and 0.12(4)). This clearly reveals that
phosphorus substitution in RbEuFe4As4 causes a decrease in its Tc, however, there is no
appreciable change in the magnetic transition temperature (TN). While single crystalline
RbEuFe4As4 exhibits ordering of the Eu2+ magnetic sublattices at TN = 15 K, the P-doped samples
order at 14.5(2) K. By comparing the observed reduction of the c-axis lattice constant and of the
cell volume upon P-substitution with results from XRD measurements under pressure [14], one
finds that the highest P-substitution level corresponds to a rather modest pressure of ~1 GPa. The
reduction in Tc by ~ 1 K is in line with this observation. However, the high-pressure studies [14,15]
also reveal an increase of TN by approximately the same amount, which we do not observe in our
P-doped samples. Possible causes may involve three-dimensional magnetic order being triggered
by magnetic exchange between Eu2+ sheets along the c-axis, across two FeAs(P) layers. In addition
to the layer spacing, this mechanism likely depends on subtle changes of the electronic structure
brought about by preferential site-occupancy by P, which would not arise in high-pressure
measurements.
Conclusion
We successfully grew X-ray diffraction quality single crystals of P-doped RbEuFe4As4
using a RbAs flux and polycrystalline samples via direct combination reactions. The amount of
phosphorus that can be doped into the RbEuFe4As4 crystal structure is limited by the preferential
As(2) site occupation by P. This phenomenon does not arise in EuFe2As2 where essentially 100%
solubility can be achieved. The smaller size of Eu2+ sublattices intercalated between the As(2) sites
renders them more accessible for P-substitution. Single crystal X-ray diffraction and Rietveld
refinements on powder diffraction data revealed that the RbEuFe4As4-xPx compositions obtained
from flux crystal growth and direct combination methods are in reasonable agreement. The
RbEuFe4As4-xPx samples showed a slight decrease in Tc with increasing P-substitution while TN
remained virtually unchanged relative to undoped RbEuFe4As4. Further in-depth analysis and
physical characterization of these materials warrants their synthesis as mm-sized single crystals,
which may be achieved by manipulating and tuning multiple reaction parameters. Achieving
higher fractions of phosphorus into the arsenic sites in the RbEuFe4As4-xPx structure is a
possibility, but it will require further clarification of the synthetic conditions. Strict kinetic control
on the crystallization process is likely necessary to access these P-richer compositions.
